o:
We must find integers L >= W with L * W = area, minimizing L - W. The best case is a square: if area is a perfect square, answer is [sqrt(area), sqrt(area)]. Otherwise we want W to be the largest divisor of area that is <= sqrt(area); then L = area / W automatically satisfies L >= W and gives the smallest gap. Constraints (area <= 10^7) mean even an O(sqrt(area)) scan of candidate widths is trivially fast.

Example 1: area = 4; divisors <= 2 are 1 and 2; the largest is 2, giving [2,2]. Example 2: area = 37 is prime; the only divisor <= sqrt(37) ≈ 6.08 is 1, so the answer is [37,1]. Example 3: area = 122122; scanning down from floor(sqrt(122122)) = 349, the first divisor found is 286, and 122122 / 286 = 427, yielding [427,286].
k: The optimal width is the largest divisor of area that does not exceed sqrt(area).
Scanning W downward from floor(sqrt(area)), the first divisor found immediately yields the minimal-difference pair.
Integer division area // W is exact when W divides area, so no floating point is needed.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over all widths
a.i: Try every width W from 1 up to sqrt(area). Whenever W divides area, record the pair [area/W, W]; keep the one with the smallest difference. Since W <= sqrt(area) guarantees L = area/W >= W, every recorded pair is valid. This works but scans more candidates than necessary.
s: Initialize best difference as infinity and result as empty.
For W from 1 while W * W <= area:
If area % W == 0, compute L = area / W and diff = L - W.
Keep the pair with the smallest diff.
a.t: O(sqrt(area)) — we test every integer up to sqrt(area).
a.sp: O(1) — only a few variables are kept.

a.n: Approach 2: Early exit from sqrt downward (optimal)
a.i: Instead of tracking the best pair, start at W = floor(sqrt(area)) and decrease until area % W == 0. The first such W is the largest divisor not exceeding sqrt(area), which by definition minimizes L - W, so we can return immediately. This avoids checking smaller divisors entirely.
a.t: O(sqrt(area)) worst case (e.g., prime area), but typically far faster since it stops at the first divisor near sqrt(area).

w: In an interview, present Approach 2 directly after stating the key insight (largest divisor <= sqrt(area)); mention Approach 1 only as a stepping stone. Pitfalls: floating-point sqrt can be off by one for large values — Python's math.isqrt or a small adjustment loop fixes this; also remember area = 1 returns [1,1] and prime areas return [area, 1]. Follow-ups might ask for all factor pairs (enumerate divisors up to sqrt) or handling very large areas where Pollard's rho factorization would be needed.
